title: What Lime’s new e-bike says about the next challenge for micromobility in DC
body:
by Erika Dutheley, Director of Government Relations in DC at Lime
This week, Lime began rolling out 1,000 of its newest shared e-bikes across the District.
Called the LimeBike, the new model features a step-through frame, smaller wheels, a lower center of gravity, an adjustable seat, and both pedal-assist and throttle options. The bike was designed to feel more approachable and comfortable for a broader range of riders. 
In my work with cities and transportation officials, I have seen how conversations about accessibility have evolved across the shared and private micromobility industries. The discussion is no longer limited to whether these transportation options are available or efficient. Increasingly, it is about whether people feel able, willing, and comfortable enough to use them.
We’ve asked our Lime riders across the District, and they are telling us the same thing.
One rider recently described using a shared e-bike to get to a volunteer event near the National Mall. Another told us that Lime “allowed me to travel with a broken foot.” Others described using Lime for doctor’s appointments, grocery trips, errands, work, and connections to the train. Their experiences show how riders rely on shared micromobility for very different reasons and at very different moments in their lives.
These riders were not looking for a new hobby. They were looking for practical ways to move around the District.
That distinction matters because shared bikes and scooters are often most useful in the spaces between other transportation options. They help connect people to transit, shorten first- and last-mile trips, and make multimodal travel more convenient when a trip does not fit neatly into a single mode of transportation.
For many riders, the value of an e-bike is that it can make everyday trips feel more manageable.
“One day, I rented a Lime bike when walking across the city became too exhausting, and it completely changed how I moved through my day. The electric assist helped me get to work, run errands, and meet friends without worrying about pain or fatigue slowing me down. For the first time in a while, I felt independent because I could travel farther and enjoy the city on my own terms.”
— Zach Z.
Many people who could benefit from an e-bike do not think of themselves as cyclists. Some have not ridden in years. Others are intimidated by traditional bike designs. Many simply want a vehicle that feels stable, intuitive, and easy to use from the moment they step on.
That feedback shapes how new vehicles are designed.
That feedback increasingly shapes how new vehicles are designed.
The LimeBike reflects years of rider feedback about comfort, confidence, and ease of use. Its step-through frame makes mounting and dismounting easier. Smaller wheels and a lower center of gravity help create a more stable feel. An adjustable seat accommodates riders of different heights, while throttle-assisted riding gives users more flexibility in how they travel.
None of those features are revolutionary on their own. Taken together, however, they point to an important shift in how the industry thinks about growth.
The next chapter of micromobility will not be defined solely by how many vehicles are available on a map. It will depend on whether more people are able to use them.
Removing barriers can take many forms. Sometimes it means lowering costs through programs like Lime Access or subscription options like LimePrime. Sometimes it means improving connections to transit. Sometimes it means designing vehicles that feel stable, intuitive, and comfortable for more riders.
The riders who rely on shared bikes and scooters are not all looking for the same thing. Some are trying to make a Metro connection. Some are looking for an affordable alternative to driving. Others simply want a transportation option that feels comfortable and easy to use.
Their stories point to the same conclusion: accessibility is not a single project or a single policy. It is an ongoing effort to remove barriers wherever they exist. As shared micromobility continues to evolve in the District, that may be the most important measure of success.

title: National links: Could cool(ing) bricks help with city heat?
body:
Students invented a brick that could reduce temperatures, but not necessarily in humid conditions. A land value tax-esque policy could help boost housing production in Washington state. Desirable lakefront property in Cleveland doesn’t need tax breaks.
Special brick could help cool cities: Industrial design students from the University of Zurich designed a terracotta brick that cools the areas around it through evaporation. In controlled environments, the bricks were able to reduce temperatures by 9°C, though the tool is less effective in humid places. Urban materials such as asphalt tend to increase surface temperatures, and tools are needed to address extreme heat. (Times of India)
Property tax reform could discourage vacant lots in Washington state: Washington state’s property tax system, standard in North America, rewards land speculation by taxing vacant lots much less than lots with productive uses. To solve this, a new report from the Center for Land Economics suggests exempting building value from the property tax. This approach would allow the state to impose a policy similar to a land value tax without violating state tax rules. (Dan Bertolet | Sightline Institute)
Cleveland’s mayor advocates development without subsidies: Mayor Justin Bibb believes the city doesn’t need to offer tax incentives on publicly-owned lakefront property in order for it to be redeveloped with private investment. The property is highly accessible to transportation, amenities, and downtown Cleveland. (Kristan Wong Karinen | Good Jobs First)
US urban areas increase housing near transit: Across the US, most large urban areas have more housing near transit now than they did four decades ago, per data available through a new Urban Institute tool. Moreover, a 10% increase in the share of housing units near transit induces 10 more transit rides per person per year. To encourage more ridership, cities must also boost transit frequency. (Yonah Freemark | Urban Institute)
Transportation reporters need stories readers care about: In a recent webinar, five reporters who focus on transportation in the US shared five lessons for how the media covers transportation. Transportation is political and broad, reporters need stories that garner engagement, every national story is local, reporters and agencies have different objectives, and relationships still matter. (Philip Plotch | Eno Center for Transportation)
Quote of the Week
“Commercial properties right now are not regulated under any stormwater permit. Think Costco, think Amazon warehouses. Large places with large parking lots are really what we’re going after.”
Sean Bothwell, executive director of California Coastkeeper Alliance in the Los Angeles Times discussing how advocates are trying to get California regulators to crack down on parking lot stormwater pollution.
This week on the Talking Headways podcast we’re joined by Jaime Benavides and Marianthi-Anna Kioumourtzoglou of Brown University to discuss their new paper showing how community severance by road infrastructure and traffic has led to more mental health-related hospital visits in New York City.

title: Washington, DC has a housing crisis. I know how to fix it
body:
Editorial note: DC’s Fair Elections regulations prohibit organizational monetary or in-kind contributions to publicly financed candidates. In keeping with these regulatory requirements, all publicly financed political candidates for District of Columbia public office can submit a pitch to Greater Greater Washington for consideration, and Greater Greater Washington subjects all such pitches to the organization’s standard editorial process.
GGWash endorsed Janeese Lewis George for DC mayor. For candidate questionnaires and endorsements across all races, visit our 2026 Elections Hub.
Washington is one of the greatest cities in the world. It is also becoming one of the most expensive places to live in America. And we are running out of time to fix it.
Average rents in the District now exceed $2,400 a month. Median home prices are approaching $700,000. Teachers, firefighters, nurses, young professionals, and the families who built this city are being pushed out. Not because they don’t love DC, but because DC has made it too expensive to stay.
I grew up in Stronghold in Northeast DC. I raised my family here and I represented Ward 5 on the DC Council for ten years before being elected At-Large in 2022. Ward 5 has historically absorbed more than its share of the city’s industrial uses, infrastructure burdens, and trash transfer stations. For too long, Ward 5 was told to take what the city needed and expect little in return. I know what it feels like when your neighborhood is left behind. I also know what it looks like when good housing projects get strangled before they ever break ground.
I watched McMillan sit undeveloped for nearly a decade while litigation dragged on. That delay didn’t just postpone more than 600 homes for Ward 5. It meant hundreds of families spent years longer waiting for housing they needed, while DC home prices climbed more than 60% between 2016 and today. I am not willing to let that happen again.
A record built on results
I have spent my career in public office rolling up my sleeves and creating pathways for more housing. As a councilmember, I introduced legislation establishing the industrial land transformation task force to unlock underutilized land for housing and economic opportunity. I also authored a law to guarantee affordable housing for lower-income households when private developers purchase District-owned land. I supported the revolving Affordable Housing Preservation Fund and fought year after year for budget funding for the Housing Production Trust Fund. 
Finally, when it became clear that our court system was being abused as a tool to stop economic growth in Stronghold, I stepped in (as I have in various ways with multiple other critical housing projects) to ensure Northeast saw the addition of those more than 600 new homes, including affordable and senior housing, a grocery store, community center with a pool, a six-acre park, and more than one million square feet of desperately needed health care space. 
As a Councilmember, I believe economic growth must always come with guard rails. That’s why I authored the Expanding Access to Justice Act, so that low-income residents facing eviction have lawyers to represent them in landlord-tenant court. I passed legislation prohibiting housing discrimination based on criminal background or arrest history, because a fair housing market means a fair shot for everyone.
That record is the foundation of my housing platform: building more housing for all and preserving our existing stock of affordable homes. According to a recent analysis from Up For Growth, we’re part of a region that has one of the highest rates of housing underproduction in the country, but it’s also a place where it’s financially feasible to build middle-income housing – if only more supportive zoning and land use regulations were in place.
Regulations account for roughly 40% of what it costs to build multifamily housing in the US. DC has the tools our neighbors lack: a Comprehensive Plan update, zoning reform authority, and a commitment to use them. As mayor, my first priority is making Washington the easiest city in the region in which to build housing.
When it comes to building income-restricted affordable housing, it’s a similar picture, which is why preservation of existing units is so important. We are spending between $700,000 and $1 million per unit to build affordable housing in this city, more than the median DC home sells for. And a study of California affordable housing projects found that every additional funding source a project requires adds approximately $6,500 per unit in transaction costs that have nothing to do with actually building the home. A typical affordable housing project in DC pieces together money from 5 to ten different sources, each with its own timeline and fees. That is a structural failure and I intend to lead us beyond reactive, one-off fixes to durable, systematic solutions.
A plan to actually build
First, we cannot fix this crisis without fixing the Comp Plan.
Litigation over what the Comp Plan says is the basis for a series of lawsuits, mostly about Ward 5 projects, that have broken the Planned Unit Development (PUD) process. Instead of the old PUD approach, we need to create a more predictable, less transactional incentive zoning structure that transparently motivates developers to produce quality assets that meet city needs without discretionary processes while still engaging communities – for example, through increased small area planning.
Most recently, the Office of Planning released a draft Future Land Use Map that would lock in the status quo of rising prices, exclusionary zoning, and displacement. A plan meant to carry this city to 2050 cannot be built around protecting segregation, widening the racial wealth gap, or Black residents leaving. I will send that map back to the Office of Planning with a clear directive: add high density housing capacity along major corridors, expand density designations to include more “missing middle” options to deploy citywide, and stop treating growth like a threat.
The Comp Plan rewrite is the single most powerful tool a mayor has to reshape this city’s housing future. I will use it to legalize rowhouses and small apartment buildings in every neighborhood, not just the handful of neighborhoods that have absorbed nearly 40% of all new housing while accounting for only about 5% of the city’s land. That concentration of growth is inequitable, with neighborhoods west of Rock Creek Park providing few new housing opportunities, and unsustainable, as the District does not have an unlimited supply of large underutilized land parcels available for redevelopment.
I will use the Comp Plan to expand transit-oriented development near both Metro stations and high-frequency bus lines, with corresponding updates to the city’s zoning code. I will eliminate parking minimums, reduce setback requirements, end floor area ratio mandates, and push for a new approach to PUDs so that projects consistent with the Comp Plan can move forward without years of litigation.
I was glad to see the current Council legalize single-stair apartment buildings up to six stories, and I further support removing elevator requirements that price small multifamily buildings out of the market entirely. I also support repealing the federal Height Act and returning authority over building heights to locally elected leaders where it belongs. My goal is preventing PUD lawsuits from advancing in court, and I will work with the Council to advance legislation modeled on the BSA language Mayor Bowser proposed in FY26 to make that a reality. Every year a project spends in court is a year families spend being shut out of housing while lawyers get paid.
I will also reform District government, especially the Department of Housing and Community Development, so that public dollars produce more homes. I will require stronger scoring for projects that produce the most bedrooms per dollar, mark

title: Breakfast links: Amazon looks to fill Helix-less Arlington block
body:
Amazon seeks temporary uses for vacant Arlington block
As Amazon’s plans for the next phase of its HQ2 remain on hold, 11 acres of open land could house art installations or athletic space. Community suggestions also included a dog park or charter bus stop. (This article is behind a paywall.)  (Douglas Fruehling / Business Journal)
Development to brings 141 homes to former DC Walter Reed campus
Canopy Row’s first batch of homes is expected for sale early next year. Overall, almost 2,000 housing units are either completed or under construction on the 66-acre campus in upper northwest.  (UrbanTurf)
Coast Guard takes over vacant offices in Prince George’s County
The six-story office building on 12.5 acres at 4700 River Road could have been redeveloped into residential units, per previous marketing. The Coast Guard’s plans for the site, formerly held by the General Services Administration, weren’t immediately clear. (This article is behind a paywall.)  (Ben Peters / Business Journal)
Congress Heights library, Metro station work advance
A new DC Public Library branch is planned to arrive next to the Congress Heights Metro in 2027. Transit work includes a reconfigured bus loop, new bus bays, sidewalks, and lighting.  (Sarah Beth Guevara / WJLA)
Walking escorts aims to protect Rockville students amid ICE presence
The effort at Meadow Hall Elementary School provides students with escorts to and from school. The school’s Hispanic population is about 60%, and the organized walks to school came to be after the school noticed fewer students walking and lower attendance at community English classes.  (Ruby Espinoza / Washington Informer)
Alexandria museum passport encourages car-free exploration
Museum-goers can land stamps from each of Historic Alexandria’s eight museums when they arrive by bus, rail, bicycle, or foot. The project comes with a mobility guide, and collecting all eight stamps unlocks a prize at the Alexandria History Museum.  (Mary Wadland / The Zebra)
Expanded July 4 fireworks could close parts of Potomac
If approved, plans from Trump allies for a world record July 4 fireworks show would place barges on the Potomac, triggering river closures that affect boaters, kayakers, and cruisers.  (Axios)
Weekend events bring road closures around the National Mall
Weekend events include the White House UFC fight and Warped Tour at the RFK Stadium grounds. As a result, DC will see road closures, especially in the federal core and around Potomac crossings.  (Christian Flores / WJLA)
Illegal driver spotted on Anacostia River Trail
A resident spotted a driver on the Anacostia River Trail earlier this week, raising safety questions about how the vehicle accessed the path used for walking, biking, and running.  (PoPville)

title: Play GGWash Junctions weekly word puzzle #50
body:
Welcome to GGWash Junctions Puzzle 50! Wow, 50! This one’s all about roads… or is it?
👉🏽 Play this week’s puzzle! 👈🏽 
💡 Need a hint?
✍🏽Volunteer to write the next puzzle!
Creating GGWash Junctions is fun and easy, and playing is even more fun when diverse authors with diverse brains create them! If you’re interested in submitting a puzzle, message me on ggwashjunctions@ggwash.org, and we’ll collab!
What is GGWash Junctions and how do you play?
GGWash Junctions is a category-matching word puzzle game similar to Connections from the New York Times, in which players divide a cluster of 16 words into four categories, each consisting of four words that share a common connection. We use a create-your-own template produced by aspiring urban planner Anthony Kenzo Salazar via his website Swellgarfo, linked here with his permission.
Detailed game instructions
You start with a grid of 16 words. Here’s an easy tutorial example:
Tutorial starting puzzle. Click to play! 

				
				
Your goal is to find four groups of four words. The words within each group share a common theme, but the theme is a mystery.
To select a group of words, click or tap on them one by one. Once you have selected a group of four words, click or tap the “submit” button.
If your answer is correct, the four words will move up from the grid into a colored rectangle, and the name of the group’s theme will pop up. If your answer is wrong, they will remain on the grid. Here’s one correct group for the tutorial:
The tutorial’s first category discovered!  

				
				
You win when you’ve discovered the themes for all four groups. Unlike NY Times Connections which limits you to four guesses, Swellgarfo’s version allows you to guess until you win.
Give that tutorial puzzle a try. The four tutorial categories are Colors, Birds, Planets, and Emotions. The scroll back up and play for real!

title: Do Something #122: Everybody’s got that person
body:
Weekly, Maryland Policy Director Dan Reed and DC Policy Director Alex Baca will share with you an action you can take in the immediate future that has the potential, sometimes great and sometimes small, to increase the number of homes in our region, decrease the trips people take by car, make all of it safer, and not screw people over in the process. Special guests Executive Director Chelsea Allinger and DC Organizer Matt Girardi join us for this week’s Do Somethings: join us for a Vision Zero happy hour; say no to widening Pennsylvania Avenue SE; and make a plan to vote in the DC and Maryland primary elections.
If you have any questions, email dreed@ggwash.org about Maryland and Virginia Do Somethings, and abaca@ggwash.org about Washington, DC, Do Somethings—or, about whatever you want to talk about.
Everyone
Join Greater Greater Washington, Washington Area Bicyclist Association, DC Families for Safe Streets, and the Coalition for Smarter Growth for a “Friends of Vision Zero” happy hour with DC Advisory Neighborhood Commissioners and members of the ANC Vision Zero Caucus June 17. Lime is generously sponsoring the meet-up—they’re bringing something new to DC, and attendees will get a sneak peak.
Whether you’re an Advisory Neighborhood Commissioner looking to coordinate with other commissioners (including prospective Commissioners!), or a resident who wants safer streets, all are welcome to join us from 6:00 pm to 8:00 pm at Sonny’s for a casual meet-up that will include optional facilitated group discussion of challenges citywide, ANC activities, and ANC-advocacy-community collaboration.
This month’s happy hour will include pizza and a round of drinks for attendees. Email event [at] ggwash.org with any questions.–CA
DC
One week to go until the primary election. Any information that you need about how to vote can be found on the Board of Elections’ website. There is much to be had under the “voters” tab of the dropdown menu!
We encourage you to vote for Janeese Lewis George for mayor, Lisa Raymond for at-large majority, Aparna Raj for Ward 1, Zachary Parker in Ward 5, Charles Allen in Ward 6, Elissa Silverman for at-large minority, and Robert White for US delegate to the House of Representatives.
See all sorts of ways to support GGWash’s endorsed candidates here, and make a financial contribution to split among our slate here.
DDOT has proposed widening Pennsylvania Avenue, and if you’re a Ward 7 resident and are not down with more urban highway widening than has already been forced upon you, plan to attend this meeting on Saturday, June 13, at 11:00 am.–MG
Maryland
Early voting in Maryland starts Thursday, June 11, meaning everybody’s reaching out to that person they turn to for voting advice. It could be a neighbor, a family member, or a trusted friend. This is the time I start getting messages, phone calls, even people showing up at my house asking: “Hey, who should I vote for?”
As someone who reads this website, you’re probably that person to somebody. More and more, I see people sharing our 2026 Elections Hub, including our candidate questionnaires and endorsements for Montgomery and Prince George’s counties. It means a lot to know that you trust us with the most powerful tool you have to make change in your community: your vote.
If you have a few minutes: Please share our endorsements for Prince George’s County Council or Montgomery County Council and Executive with someone you know who’s planning to vote.
If you have a few more minutes: check out our post listing ways to help our endorsed candidates, which we’re updating constantly. The big opportunities to support our endorsees are in Montgomery County: Drew Morrison, who’s running for County Council in District 1 (Bethesda and Potomac), Kate Stewart, councilmember from District 4 (Takoma Park, Silver Spring, and North Bethesda) and Council President Natali Fani-González, who represents District 6 (Wheaton and Aspen Hill), are all hosting canvasses each weekend through the election June 23.
Finally: many but not all of our endorsees use ActBlue, so we’ve set up links where you can make a donation that’s split among them:
Montgomery County: Andrew Friedson, Jim McNulty, Drew Morrison, and Dawn Luedtke
Prince George’s County: Sydney Harrison, Jolene Ivey, Eric Olson, and Martin Mitchell
Two weeks to go! We’re so close.–DR
Your support of GGWash enables us, Dan and Alex, to do our jobs. Our jobs are knowing how development and planning works in DC, Maryland, and Virginia. If it’s appropriate to take action to advance our goals, which we hope you share, we can let you know what will have the most impact, and how to do it well. You can make a financial contribution to GGWash here. And if you want to see Do Something in your inbox, scroll down and sign up for our daily emails.

title: Ward 7 deserves a Pennsylvania Avenue that works for everyone
body:
If you have ever driven, biked, walked, or waited for a bus at the intersection of Pennsylvania and Minnesota Avenue SE, you already know the problem. It is chaotic, confusing, and unsafe. The community has known this for years, and so has the District Department of Transportation, which is why the Pennsylvania Ave SE and Minnesota Ave SE Intersection Safety Improvement Project has been nearly two decades in the making.
ANC 7B wants this intersection fixed. Let me be unambiguous about that, because it seems to get lost in the back-and-forth: We are not trying to kill this project. We are trying to make sure that after 19 years of planning, what gets built actually serves the people who live here.
So far, we are not confident it will.
A process that got off on the wrong foot
The first version of DDOT’s design would have severed access from Pennsylvania Avenue to 25th Street, a route used by WMATA bus route D10 and the only street in the immediate area with a bike lane. Unprotected as it is, cutting it off would have eliminated the one available exit from this chaotic intersection onto a street where cyclists are at least nominally accounted for.
When ANC 7B formally disapproved the plan in March, DDOT began implementing it anyway — just one business day after the public comment period closed. The comment period closed on a Friday; construction began Monday morning. After we raised the alarm and engaged Ward 7 Councilmember Wendell Felder’s office, DDOT stopped, rolled back the changes, and agreed to revise the design. The updated plan keeps 25th Street open, a real win. In April, ANC 7B passed a resolution of conditional support outlining what else we needed to see: rush-hour bus lanes on Pennsylvania Avenue between Prout and 27th Streets, converting to parking during non-peak hours, and protected bike infrastructure throughout the project scope.
None of those conditions were met.
The 10-lane problem and why it’s a showstopper
When DDOT returned to the ANC in May, they didn’t send the designers. They sent the builders to tell us construction starts in June. The new design retained what has emerged as our most fundamental objection: extending the left-turn lanes from eastbound Pennsylvania Avenue to northbound Minnesota Avenue, expanding the 2300 block of Pennsylvania Avenue from eight lanes to 10. This is a nonstarter for ANC 7B, and the community has been unequivocal about it.
DDOT insisted these aren’t “new lanes” because they are turning lanes, not travel lanes. That distinction does not hold up for a pedestrian trying to cross the street. The design creates 11 points where a pedestrian can encounter a vehicle: 10 lanes, plus a right turn from L’Enfant Square feeding directly into the crosswalk. That crosswalk will be controlled by a pedestrian-only signal, the kind drivers are far more likely to ignore since there is no risk of hitting another vehicle and these signals are rarely camera-enforced.
DDOT argues the design is necessary because drivers exiting 295 currently cause crashes trying to cut across four lanes to reach the left-turn lane onto Minnesota Avenue. We understand the problem. But the 295/Pennsylvania Avenue interchange is not being modified in this project, meaning those same drivers will now need to cross five or six lanes instead of four. It is hard to see how that is safer. When I asked DDOT to name another neighborhood arterial in DC carrying 10 lanes of traffic, they could not. Ward 7 residents should not have to serve as the District’s test case to find out what happens when you put 10 lanes through a neighborhood.
A road that works against its own neighborhood
In FY2021, the DC Council funded the Pennsylvania Avenue East Small Area Plan to spark economic development along Pennsylvania Avenue from the John Philip Sousa Bridge to the Maryland border. The 2300 block, the very block at the center of this redesign, is part of the plan’s first phase.
Businesses only thrive when customers can reach them. Right now, that is a problem: Pedestrians don’t feel safe due to chaotic traffic, cyclists have no protected infrastructure, buses crawl through congestion, and there is nowhere to park to stop and shop. The community’s vision addresses all of this. DDOT’s does not, and the design makes future improvements harder, not easier. Under the current proposal, the median would be significantly reduced to accommodate two additional turning lanes — and it is precisely where protected bike infrastructure should go. Once that space is gone, so is that opportunity. The Council invested in a plan for this neighborhood’s future. The intersection redesign should be consistent with that vision, not in conflict with it.
Two issues, not one
DDOT has at times treated all of our objections as equivalent. They are not.
On bus and bike infrastructure, we accept that federal funding restrictions are real under the current administration. We are not asking DDOT to violate those rules. We are asking for a written commitment, with a timeline, for when these improvements will follow using local dollars. A promise without a deadline is not a plan — and communities east of the river have a long memory for promises that never materialize. We are always told our turn is coming; it never seems to come.
On the lane expansion, there is no federal constraint in play. That is a choice, and it is the wrong one. Residents at community association meetings have said they would rather see the funding lost entirely than accept a 10-lane road in their community. That is how strongly people feel, and it is why this remains a showstopper regardless of what else is resolved.
Our asks are straightforward: remove the lane expansion, commit in writing to a timeline for bus and bike improvements, and build something consistent with the small area plan the council already funded. That is what we are asking for, and it is not unreasonable.
A community meeting is scheduled for June 13 at 11:00 am at the DC Dream Center (2826 Q Street SE), co-hosted by ANC 7B and ANC 8A. Virtual attendance is available here. If you care about how this intersection gets built, and you should, we hope to see you there.
Top image: Pennsylvania and Minnesota Avenues SE. Image from Google Maps.

title: Breakfast links: Maryland parks agency sues over fund transfers in Prince George’s County
body:
Lawsuit contests funding decisions affecting parks in Prince George’s County
The lawsuit from the Maryland-National Capital Park and Planning Commission accuses Prince George’s County of illegally retaining tens of millions of dollars meant for the commission. Instead, the county reportedly plans to use that money to support its budget.  (Dave Leval / DC News Now, NBC4)
Fairfax County to test 20 mph speed limits
A pilot program will reduce speed limits from 25 mph to 20 mph on up to nine residential or business district roads. The program will start with three roads this summer that will be evaluated through early 2027.  (Scott McCaffrey / FFXnow)
Affordable apartments set to break ground in Burrville
The publicly-funded 56-unit development at 950 Eastern Avenue NE finalized its financing, which includes $23.8 million in tax-exempt bonds. The five-story building will have 43 units for households earning 50% or less of the area median income and 13 permanent supportive housing units for formerly unhoused residents. (This article is behind a paywall.)  (Alan Kline / Business Journal)
County manager recommends rejection of Arlington historic district
The County Board will vote June 17 on whether to create a historic district at a property in Aurora Highlights, undermining an approved five-story affordable housing project there. County Manager Mark Schwartz’s recommendation aligns with county staff but differs from the Historical Affairs and Landmark Review Board’s 7-4 vote for the district.   (Scott McCaffrey / ARLnow)
Federal government sells DC’s Old Post Office building
The building’s current leaseholder bought the land and building at 1100 Pennsylvania Avenue NW for a reported $80 million. The building could go on to sell for up to $400 million.  (Tracy Johnke / WTOP)
Sewer line emergency repairs look to protect Maryland, DC drinking water
DC Water will soon start emergency repairs on part of the Potomac Interceptor sewer line in Potomac, Maryland after inspections found corrosion and exposed rebar. A spill at this location could harm Maryland and DC drinking water supplies.  (Neal Augenstein / WTOP)
